ch01.point: The manifest space is not a set of false beliefs. It is a set of true observations attached to a false engine — which is why it survives refutation.
ch01.do: Name which of the four needs it meets in you, or in someone you love: agency, method, desire, beauty.
ch01.next: A system held together by a grammar cannot be answered one sentence at a time. So we need the grammar.

ch02.point: Manifestation is a grammar of seven rules, not a doctrine of one claim — and every rule has an author and a date. Refute a sentence and the grammar produces another; date the grammar and it becomes convertible.
ch02.do: Listen for the seven rules in the next piece of manifestation content you meet — and count how many are actually present.
ch02.next: A grammar implies a theology. Read the manifest space as a system, and it has every part but one.

ch03.point: The manifest space is a complete rival account of God, creation, person, sin, salvation, revelation, church, sacrament and last things — with a hole where the creator should be.
ch03.do: Write down which of its nine positions you have heard preached, approvingly, from a Catholic pulpit.
ch03.next: It spreads because it works. Not as it claims — but really.

ch04.point: It succeeds because it meets four real needs badly, in a culture that stopped meeting them well. An answer that does not meet them better will lose.
ch04.do: Identify the one need your parish meets worst, and write one thing you could do about it this month.
ch04.next: The Church has faced a rival account of everything before, and it did not begin with a ban.

ch05.point: Aristotle arrived as a complete system and the first institutional response was prohibition. The prohibition failed, because you cannot ban a better tool.
ch05.do: Read one primary text of the movement you are tempted to dismiss, all the way through, before you say another word about it.
ch05.next: What replaced the ban was a method — six moves, in order.

ch06.point: Thomas described before he judged, separated the instrument from the metaphysics, subordinated the instrument, corrected from within, refused by name, and institutionalised. Six moves, in that order.
ch06.do: Apply move one to a practice you dislike: state it in a form its practitioners would accept. If you cannot, you are not ready for move five.
ch06.next: The method has a bill, and it is usually presented to the person who did the work.

ch07.point: Every integration is condemned by the guardians before it is received by the institution. Thomas in 1277, Faustina in 1959, and the catechist in your parish on Tuesday.
ch07.do: Decide now, in writing, what you will do when you are misrepresented: stay inside, publish the method, do not monetise.
ch07.next: The audit begins. Four tests, then fourteen verdicts.

ch08.point: Four tests — Creator and creature, nature and grace, cross and glory, Church and self — and each can be asked as a question a real person can answer.
ch08.do: Ask the four questions of your own practice, not of someone else's.
ch08.next: The first test is the deepest, and it is the one that dissolves the whole vocabulary.

ch09.point: Almost every error in the manifest space is a refusal of analogy: a single univocal word — energy, alignment, frequency — doing the work of a doctrine.
ch09.do: Take one word. Write what it means in physics, what it means in your speech, and what it means in the Creed.
ch09.next: The second test is about grace, and it is where the system's Pelagianism shows.

ch10.point: The manifest space is a total, cheerful Pelagianism: agency without givenness, effort without gift, and therefore performance without mercy.
ch10.do: Identify one thing you do in order to earn what has already been given, and stop doing it for a week.
ch10.next: The third test is the one that decides the verdict, and it cannot be repaired.

ch11.point: The system cannot allow the sufferer to be innocent, and the failure is structural. It is refuted by John 9, by Job, and by the Cross.
ch11.do: Learn the four sentences for the sick by heart, and say none of them until you are sitting down.
ch11.next: The same failure appears in its account of other people.

ch12.point: "Everyone is you pushed out" is the logical consequence of the system's premises, and it abolishes the other person — and therefore love.
ch12.do: Ask who you ask to pray for you, other than yourself. If the answer is no one, you have found the real work.
ch12.next: With the tests in place, the claims can be judged one by one.

ch13.point: Four claims are true and should be taught louder; three name something real and must be corrected; seven are false and cannot be repaired inside the system.
ch13.do: Pick the one claim you actually hold, and test it against its verdict. Do not pick the one you find easiest to reject.
ch13.next: The argument will be won or lost at the level of vocabulary.

ch14.point: Inculturation succeeds or fails at the level of the lexicon: thirty words carry the system, and most of them are equivocal.
ch14.do: Choose one word from the lexicon and learn its Catholic meaning well enough to explain it to a fourteen-year-old.
ch14.next: None of which changes anyone by itself, because refutation is not conversion.

ch15.point: People are not changed by arguments. They are changed by a practice and by a person — and mostly in that order.
ch15.do: Stop arguing with someone about manifestation, and hand her one practice with a time attached.
ch15.next: And so we turn from what is wrong to what we actually have.

ch16.point: "Manifestation" is a biblical word, and in Scripture it is something God does. The manifest space has the shape of revelation turned inside out.
ch16.do: Read Romans 8:19 and Colossians 3:3–4 today, slowly, out loud.
ch16.next: The purpose clause is three words long, and it reorders everything.

ch17.point: The manifestation of the Spirit is given, to each, for the common good — three words that no spiritual market can survive.
ch17.do: Ask "who is this for?" about the thing you most want, and write the answer down.
ch17.next: The world itself is waiting for the same thing.

ch18.point: The world is a creature in labour, not a mirror of your interior. Which is why the Church is more materialist than the market.
ch18.do: Treat one created thing this week as a companion rather than a surface: a body, an animal, a piece of ground, a person who serves you.
ch18.next: And the manifestation you are waiting for is currently hidden.

ch19.point: Your life is hidden with Christ in God. The hiddenness is not the failure of the manifestation; it is its location.
ch19.do: Name one hidden thing in your life and thank God for it, out loud, without asking him to make it visible.
ch19.next: Hidden things are carried by matter, and matter is the Church's speciality.

ch20.point: The sacraments are efficacious signs, not techniques: the one who acts is Christ, and the efficacy is a promise kept, not a formula performed.
ch20.do: On Sunday, touch the water on the way in deliberately, and know what you are doing.
ch20.next: The word itself runs the other way: disclosure, not projection.

ch21.point: The manifestation of conscience is the exact inversion of the manifest space: not the interior projected onto the world, but the interior disclosed to a witness.
ch21.do: Tell one person one true thing about your interior life this week. Not a confession of sin necessarily — a disclosure.
ch21.next: Which brings us to the engine room of the whole doctrine.

ch22.point: Providence governs through real secondary causes, which is why your action is serious and why the outcome is not your responsibility.
ch22.do: Divide your current worry into two columns: mine to do, and not mine. Do the first; hand over the second.
ch22.next: Providence makes room for desire — and desire needs purifying.

ch23.point: Desire is a signpost, not an oracle: it tells you what you love, and what you love may be false.
ch23.do: Take one desire and ask the three questions: what is this for, who else does it touch, would I take it from God's hand.
ch23.next: What forms a person is not the desire but the habit.

ch24.point: The law of assumption is true about persons and false about the world. Aquinas's account of habitus is the true version, and grace is the true assumption.
ch24.do: Write a rule of three practices: one daily, one weekly, one monthly. Small enough that you will actually keep them.
ch24.next: Which is why the rest of the book is practice.

ch25.point: Human beings are formed by what they do repeatedly. Doctrine alone has never displaced a devotion, and it will not displace this one.
ch25.do: Pick one practice and one time, and put it in your calendar as an appointment you cannot move.
ch25.next: But not every practice is Catholic. Six marks tell the difference.

ch26.point: A Catholic practice is addressed to a person, mediated by the Church, embodied, rhythmic, non-manipulative, and ordered to communion.
ch26.do: Test your favourite devotion against the six marks. Where it fails, ask whether the fault is the devotion or your way of doing it.
ch26.next: Word and image come first, because that is where the manifest space is strongest.

ch27.point: Keep the technique and change the addressee: the petition, the aspiration, the composition of place, the altar, the name.
ch27.do: Write the petition tonight, with the three questions under it, and date it.
ch27.next: Then there is the body, and the clock.

ch28.point: The manifest space has improvised a calendar, a night prayer, and a bodily discipline out of nothing. The Church has better versions of all three, unused.
ch28.do: Keep Compline for seven nights. Five minutes. Use a book or an app; do not improvise.
ch28.next: Then the hardest material: memory, and the shadow.

ch29.point: The past is not rewritten; it is forgiven, healed, and recorded. Confession does what revision claims, and keeps the fact.
ch29.do: Go to confession within the fortnight, and bring one thing you have been carrying for years.
ch29.next: And the signs? They are not a code.

ch30.point: The Church forbids decoding omens and offers something better: the discernment of movements, tested over time and by counsel.
ch30.do: Start the movements log tonight. Three columns, five days, no interpretation on day one.
ch30.next: Put the pieces together into a rite you can actually pray.

ch31.point: The nine days move from asking to thanksgiving, and day five is the pivot: *what if the answer is no?* A prayer that can survive that question is a prayer; a technique cannot survive it at all.
ch31.do: Begin the nine days tonight, with one intention and one sentence you will say even when it is hard.
ch31.next: But most people will meet this book in a conversation, not in a novena.

ch32.point: Two questions, three colours, one rule: at the bedside, presence only.
ch32.do: Learn the two questions by heart. They do most of the work and they cost nothing.
ch32.next: Which brings us from the person to the institution.

ch33.point: The first institutional act is description: the Moerbeke work of reading the thing closely enough to state it in terms its practitioners accept.
ch33.do: Interview one practitioner this month, and do not correct anything during the interview.
ch33.next: Which produces a body of work, if the genre is right.

ch34.point: The disputed question is honest by construction: the objections are printed above the answer, so the reader can see whether the answer survives them.
ch34.do: Write the strongest objection to your own position, in the objector's voice, and read it to someone who agrees with her.
ch34.next: Ideas do not survive on their merits; they survive in institutions.

ch35.point: A centre, a journal, a formation module, a free library, a community, a network of directors, and a diocesan desk — with five rules of governance.
ch35.do: Name the one institution you could actually influence in the next two years, and write down how.
ch35.next: And how would we know whether any of it was working?

ch36.point: The Church's criteria — prayer, conversion, charity, freedom — are better than the market's, and they can be measured without turning holiness into a number.
ch36.do: Run the ten-item instrument on yourself, honestly, and keep the score somewhere you will find it in a year.
ch36.next: Which leaves the timescale, and the expectation of failure.

ch37.point: Expect to be ignored, condemned, co-opted, partially received, or absorbed — in that order of likelihood — and plan for fifty years.
ch37.do: Decide what you will do in the first two years, and what you will refuse to do at any point.
ch37.next: And now the objections, beginning with the ones from our own side.

ch38.point: Each objection from the tradition is true in its warning and false in its conclusion: a real danger, a non sequitur, and a counsel of inaction.
ch38.do: Pick the objection that stings most, and answer it in writing, in private, before you answer it in public.
ch38.next: The objections from the other side are sharper.

ch39.point: Two objections have real force — that prayer is manifestation with extra steps, and that the mystics said the same thing — and both are answered by a life rather than by an argument.
ch39.do: Answer "it works for me" with compassion the next time you hear it: keep the practice, change the explanation.
ch39.next: Which brings us back to the girl at eleven-eleven.

ch40.point: You are not creating reality, your desire is not an oracle, there is someone listening who can say no, and what you are waiting for is the manifestation of the children of God.
ch40.do: Five minutes tonight: the name of Jesus, the thing you actually want, and "not my will but yours." Then sleep.
ch40.next: Nothing. The book is finished; the appendices are the apparatus — a triage card, a pilot protocol, forty questions still open, and an index for the reader who wants to argue.
